job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Jade Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake early, because the house is busy. My grandmother Kamla likes tea at six and my mother leaves for the family pharmacy by eight. I send applications in the morning and then I go to the pharmacy and do the books, which my father has let me take over since I graduated. I studied accounting at De Montfort in Leicester, finished with a first in June, and interned at a small local accountancy practice and at a building society. Evenings are family, the temple on Thursdays, and sometimes a long walk with my cousin Anjali.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible. Big claims usually shrink once people try the thing. I'd say to my father at the pharmacy that the stock system will stay the same, and that we shouldn't spend money on gadgets we don't need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel comfortable. Plenty of firms in Leicester still need people who can read a ledger and answer the phone. My worry isn't AI, it's that I've done everything right and nothing has come yet. The practice where I interned says there might be an opening in the new year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd go to the practice every other week, so they remember my face, and keep the pharmacy books tidy. I'd apply to the building society's graduate programme again. I'd also save a little more each month, because my father taught me that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly peaceful. I trust that things work out. But there's a small knot, because I'm 23 and everyone at the temple asks about my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the one pressure in your life right now that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The questions. I love my community, but every Thursday at the temple somebody's auntie asks if I've still got no job. I smile and say soon. I know they mean well, but I feel I should have a title by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who around you would you talk to about the job search, and what would they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father, who says to be patient and work in the pharmacy meanwhile. My cousin Anjali, who's a nurse and says to take any job and move later. I prefer my father's advice, since the pharmacy books are real work and it's useful.

I'd tell my father we shouldn't spend on **gadgets** we don't need.

Reapply to the building society's **graduate programme**.
feel: **Peaceful** mostly, with a small knot when people at the temple ask about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine to use new tools, but not to throw people out. In my family's pharmacy we've watched the dispensing system change and the staff stay. I'd say firms should look after the people they have, and I'd say it at the temple too, where people listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my entry-level job shrinks. At the practice, the juniors did the bank reconciliations and tax returns for small customers, and a program could do much of it. I don't use any of these tools. If I'm honest, I'd rather not learn them, but I might have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the practice and ask the senior partner, Mr Desai, how he sees it and what he'd want from a junior. I'd probably learn one of the tools, slowly, with Anjali's help. And I'd offer to take on more of the pharmacy's accounts so my family's business has fewer outside costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the sort of thing that makes me feel I have to move before I'm ready. I like to see something working for a year before I trust it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry-level tasks in your field would go first, and what does that do to a job like the one you want?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bank reconciliations, tax returns for simple customers, and invoice entry. Those were the jobs of a junior at the practice. What stays is the work that needs trust. The family who bring a shoebox of papers want to talk to somebody, and that part of the job stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who graduated a year after you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to build trust with a small firm or a family business, where the customer wants a person. And to learn one tool, just one, so they're not seen as stuck. I'd also tell them to keep faith, but not to wait for a miracle.

I'd say firms should **look after** the people they have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and we need to protect families first. I'd say at the temple that we should look after each other, as we always have. I'd also say governments must act on support quickly, because families can't carry it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be very frightened. If machines do all thinking work, my degree is in exactly the wrong thing. I'd worry for my father's pharmacy too, because the paperwork side and the dispensing could be taken. I'd think about what the family could do together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my father and say we should plan together. The pharmacy might need to cut costs and I'd offer to work there for free if needed. I'd put my savings in a safe place, and I'd go to the community leaders to see what help exists. I'd learn something hands-on, probably, like pharmacy dispensing, since that's near us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel the earth shift. I'm used to a world where hard work gets rewarded, and this would break that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what changes about how you spend the next few months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say sit down with the family. We'd write what we have and what we need. My father would say pray and plan, and he'd be right on both. I'd also ask my aunt in Birmingham about care training for evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your family the night this was confirmed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my parents that I'm not afraid, even if I am. I'd say I'll work at the pharmacy and it's our business, and we do it together. My grandmother would pray and I'd cry later.

say: I'd say we must **protect families first** and look after each other.
I'd say governments must **act quickly** on support.
think: If machines do all thinking work, my degree is in **exactly the wrong thing**.
I'd worry for my father's **pharmacy** too.

feel: **Alarmed**: a world where hard work is rewarded would break.
S2.quote: I'm used to a world where hard work gets rewarded, and this would break that.
fieldNote: Her **faith and family** are her first response, then practical help.

steps.text: Sit down with her father to plan pharmacy costs and jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to care for people. I'd say that families should plan, like we plan for weddings, with the whole family in the room. At the temple I'd say we should help our young ones train for jobs with people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get a first job and then it's up to me to make it count. I'd be nervous but not panicking. I'd want to move into work with trust, perhaps a family business adviser. That's the kind of accounting that's about people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take any good offer, work hard and save at least a third. I'd also take a short course in tax planning for family businesses, which small shops need. I'd keep helping at the pharmacy, because it's both income and a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a threat, but I can plan around it. A five-year plan is a thing I know how to make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years of warning, what would you do differently from the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be in a panic. With five years I'd carry on, but wisely. I'd also help Anjali, who's a nurse, think about what she might do, because the family is the real insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd stop doing, or start doing, that you wouldn't if it were sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop thinking of accounting as a numbers job and start thinking of it as advice for families. And I'd talk to my father about when to let the pharmacy hire help, and when to keep it ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is generous, so let's use it wisely. I'd say we should teach the young to value honest work and people skills. At home I'd say the same, because my parents built the pharmacy slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly safe. By 33 I'd have had a career, maybe a family, and I'd have my own accounts business or a role at the pharmacy. The change would reach my children more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work at a good firm for several years, pass the chartered exams and keep helping at the pharmacy. I'd save for a flat near my parents. And I'd try the tools when the practice I work for proves they're good, not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long time, and I trust that people will find a way. I'd also pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do with the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry, probably, and plan children around it. I'd want my children to learn people skills and a trade as well as school. The decade would be about setting a good base, not rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having a decade make you feel safe, or does it just push the worry further off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels safe in a sensible way. It doesn't make the worry go. A decade can pass quickly, and I'd want to keep checking it, with my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time for a family to plan or for me to find another path, and everything I've done could be pointless. What would help is community support, a plan from government for training, and people to tell the truth about it. And I'd like my father's pharmacy to be safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think resistant means stubborn. For me it means careful. I want to see a thing work before I trust it. That's how my family built what we have.

headlineQuote: People think resistant means stubborn. For me it means careful. I want to see a thing work before I trust it.
portrait: Jade is 23, a **top graduate** in accounting from Leicester who lives with her parents and grandmother.
She keeps the **family pharmacy's books** and leans on faith, family and community.
She never uses AI tools and wants to see a thing work before she trusts it.
Her moods run from uneasy to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, where family is her first answer.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, with no time for her family to plan or for her to find another path.
whatWouldHelp: **Community support**, a government training plan, honesty about the change, and a safe family pharmacy.
